positions/free-will-defence/oneLine: Evil is not a created substance but a privation of good, arising from the misuse of free will by angels and humans in a world God made good; God permits it because a world with free creatures is better, and he brings greater good out of evil.
positions/free-will-defence/coreClaims/0: Everything God made is good; evil is a lack or corruption of good (privatio boni).
positions/free-will-defence/coreClaims/1: Moral evil comes from the free choices of angels and humans; natural evil is linked to the fall.
positions/free-will-defence/coreClaims/2: Free will is a great good that God does not override.
positions/free-will-defence/coreClaims/3: God permits evil only because he can bring good even out of it.
positions/free-will-defence/coreClaims/4: Modern “defence” (Plantinga) argues only that God and evil are logically compatible.
positions/free-will-defence/origin: Developed by Augustine against Manichaean dualism (On Free Choice of the Will, 388-395; Enchiridion 421); dominant in Western theology; revived in analytic form by Alvin Plantinga’s free-will defence (1965, 1974).
positions/free-will-defence/strongestArg: It maintains God’s goodness and the goodness of creation while taking sin with full seriousness.
Plantinga’s defence is widely regarded as having answered the logical problem of evil (that God and evil are contradictory).
It coheres with the biblical narrative of creation, fall and redemption.
positions/free-will-defence/strongestObj: Critics argue that natural evils (earthquakes, disease, animal suffering before humans existed) are hard to blame on human free will.
Compatibilists ask why God could not create free creatures who always choose good.
Hick and others object that a perfectly good creature’s fall is unintelligible, and the fall-narrative conflicts with evolutionary history.
positions/free-will-defence/responses/0: Defenders extend the argument to fallen angels (Plantinga, Lewis) or to the cost of a law-governed world.
positions/free-will-defence/responses/1: Plantinga answers that it is possible that every free creature God could create would go wrong somewhere (“transworld depravity”).
positions/free-will-defence/consequences: Shaped Western liturgy, preaching and confession.
Remains the most widely used framework in popular apologetics.
positions/skeptical-theism/oneLine: Since human beings are in no position to grasp all the goods and evils, and their connections, that an infinite God might know, our failure to see a reason for a particular evil is not good evidence that there is none.
positions/skeptical-theism/coreClaims/0: The inference from “I see no reason for this evil” to “there is no reason” is unreliable.
positions/skeptical-theism/coreClaims/1: The gap between divine and human understanding is like that between a parent and an infant.
positions/skeptical-theism/coreClaims/2: The book of Job models trust without explanation.
positions/skeptical-theism/coreClaims/3: This undercuts the evidential argument from evil without offering a full theodicy.
positions/skeptical-theism/origin: Formulated in analytic philosophy by Stephen Wykstra (“The Humean Obstacle”, 1984) in response to William Rowe’s evidential argument (1979); developed by William Alston, Michael Bergmann and Alvin Plantinga.
positions/skeptical-theism/strongestArgu: It reflects the biblical humility of Job and Paul.
It is a modest, logically careful claim that does not trivialise suffering by offering glib explanations.
It effectively blocks the premise of Rowe’s evidential argument.
positions/skeptical-theism/strongestObje: Critics argue that if we cannot judge God’s reasons, we also cannot infer God’s goodness or trust his promises (moral scepticism).
Others say it can make moral action impossible: if any evil might serve a hidden good, why prevent it?
Protest theodicists find it pastorally cold.
positions/skeptical-theism/responses/0: Skeptical theists answer that their scepticism is limited to the total realm of goods and evils, not basic moral knowledge or revealed promises.
positions/skeptical-theism/responses/1: They argue our duty to prevent evil comes from God’s command, not from calculating outcomes.
positions/skeptical-theism/consequences/: Became a major option in philosophy of religion after 1984.
Influenced pastoral emphasis on lament and trust.
positions/protest-theodicy/oneLine: In face of horrendous evil such as the Holocaust, explanations that justify God are morally inadequate; faith takes the form of lament, protest and argument with God, together with resistance to evil.
positions/protest-theodicy/coreClaims/0: Theodicies risk justifying the unjustifiable and silencing victims.
positions/protest-theodicy/coreClaims/1: The biblical tradition of lament (Job, Psalms, Habakkuk) legitimises protest against God.
positions/protest-theodicy/coreClaims/2: Faith after Auschwitz must keep faith with victims.
positions/protest-theodicy/coreClaims/3: Practical resistance to evil matters more than theoretical explanation.
positions/protest-theodicy/origin: Rooted in Jewish responses to the Shoah (Elie Wiesel’s The Trial of God, 1979); articulated for Christians by John K. Roth (“A Theodicy of Protest”, 1981), Dorothee Sölle, Johann Baptist Metz and, in related form, by Kenneth Surin’s critique of theodicy (1986). Jürgen Moltmann’s The Crucified God (1972) relocated suffering in God.
positions/protest-theodicy/strongestArgu: It refuses to make suffering “make sense” in ways that wound victims.
It recovers the neglected biblical genre of lament.
It keeps theology accountable to history, especially Christian complicity in antisemitism.
positions/protest-theodicy/strongestObje: Classical theists object that protest against God either presupposes his goodness (making protest self-undermining) or denies it.
Others argue that refusing theodicy abandons the intellectual task of faith.
Some worry it slides toward a limited or culpable God.
positions/protest-theodicy/responses/0: Roth replies that protest is a form of faith that holds God to his promises, as Job did.
positions/protest-theodicy/responses/1: Supporters argue that theodicy as a theoretical enterprise is a modern invention (post-Leibniz) and that the older tradition practised lament and hope.
positions/protest-theodicy/consequences/: Influenced Jewish–Christian dialogue and post-Holocaust theology.
Renewed liturgical use of lament psalms.
positions/amillennialism/oneLine: The thousand years of Revelation 20 symbolise Christ’s present reign with his saints between his first and second comings; there will be one return, one general resurrection and one judgement.
positions/amillennialism/coreClaims/0: Satan was "bound" by Christ’s victory at his first coming so that the gospel can go to the nations (Matt 12:29; Rev 20:2–3).
positions/amillennialism/coreClaims/1: The "first resurrection" is the new birth or the souls of martyrs reigning with Christ in heaven; the "second" is the bodily resurrection at the end.
positions/amillennialism/coreClaims/2: Revelation is a book of symbols and recapitulating visions, not a strict chronology; chapter 20 restates the whole Church age.
positions/amillennialism/coreClaims/3: Christ returns once, at the end of history, to raise all the dead, judge the world and inaugurate the new creation.
positions/amillennialism/coreClaims/4: Good and evil grow together until the harvest (Matt 13:24–30); no earthly golden age precedes the end.
positions/amillennialism/origin: Developed from Alexandrian criticism of literal chiliasm (Origen, Dionysius of Alexandria) and the Donatist exegete Tyconius (c.380), it was given classic form by Augustine in City of God 20 (c.425–426) and became the standard view of Western and Eastern churches alike. The term "amillennial" itself is a 20th-century coinage; many adherents prefer to call it "realized millennialism".
positions/amillennialism/strongestArgume: Revelation is pervasively symbolic (numbers, beasts, a lamb with seven horns), so a literal 1,000 years is the least consistent reading of a single passage.
The rest of the New Testament teaches one coming, one resurrection of "all that are in the graves" (John 5:28–29) and one judgement, with no intermediate earthly kingdom.
It best explains why every major historic church confession and liturgy, East and West, affirms Christ’s return and judgement without any millennium.
The New Testament repeatedly locates believers’ present reign and resurrection "with Christ" now (Eph 2:6; Col 3:1; Rev 1:6), matching Revelation 20:4–6.
positions/amillennialism/strongestObject: The same verb "came to life" (ezesan) is used of both resurrections in Rev 20:4–5; reading the first spiritually and the second bodily is, as Henry Alford put it (1868), exegetically arbitrary.
Satan hardly looks "bound" now, since the New Testament also calls him a roaring lion (1 Pet 5:8) and "god of this world" (2 Cor 4:4).
It allegedly spiritualises Old Testament promises of a renewed land and Davidic kingdom that the earliest Christians (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus) took literally.
Critics say its post-Constantinian rise reflects a Church comfortable with power rather than pure exegesis.
positions/amillennialism/responses/0: Amillennialists answer that the binding is specific: Satan cannot "deceive the nations" so as to stop the gospel (Rev 20:3), which is compatible with his continued hostility.
positions/amillennialism/responses/1: John 5:25–29 itself uses "live" in two senses (spiritual and bodily) within a few verses, so the shift in Rev 20 is not arbitrary.
positions/amillennialism/responses/2: Old Testament promises are fulfilled, not cancelled, in Christ and in the new creation (2 Cor 1:20; Heb 11:10–16; Rev 21–22), which is more, not less, literal than a temporary millennium.
positions/amillennialism/responses/3: Origen and Dionysius rejected chiliasm well before Constantine, and Justin admits many orthodox Christians in his day did not hold it.
positions/amillennialism/consequences/0: Fixed the Western and Eastern Church in a non-chronological reading of Revelation for over a millennium.
positions/amillennialism/consequences/1: Identified the Church’s present life with Christ’s kingdom, which could legitimise ecclesiastical power (Christendom) but also relativised all earthly regimes as passing (the two cities).
positions/amillennialism/consequences/2: Encouraged sacramental and liturgical, rather than calendrical, eschatology: the Eucharist as foretaste of the age to come.
positions/amillennialism/consequences/3: Underlies the confessional rejection of chiliasm (Augsburg XVII; Second Helvetic 11).
positions/postmillennialism/oneLine: Christ will return after a long "millennium" of gospel triumph in which the Spirit converts the nations and the world is largely Christianised.
positions/postmillennialism/coreClaims/0: The kingdom of God grows gradually like a mustard seed and leaven until it fills the world (Matt 13:31–33; Dan 2:35).
positions/postmillennialism/coreClaims/1: The Great Commission will substantially succeed: most nations and peoples will be converted before the end.
positions/postmillennialism/coreClaims/2: The millennium is a future (or progressively arriving) golden age of righteousness and peace within history, not necessarily a literal 1,000 years.
positions/postmillennialism/coreClaims/3: Christ returns at the close of this age for one general resurrection and judgement.
positions/postmillennialism/coreClaims/4: Christians should therefore work with confidence for revival, missions and social reform.
positions/postmillennialism/origin: Elements appear in Eusebius’ Constantinian optimism and in Puritan hopes (Thomas Brightman, 1615) for the conversion of the Jews and a latter-day glory. It was systematised by the Anglican Daniel Whitby (Treatise of the True Millennium, 1703) and became the dominant Anglo-American Protestant view through Jonathan Edwards and the Great Awakenings, lasting until the First World War.
positions/postmillennialism/proponentsOt: R. J. Rushdoony and Greg Bahnsen (theonomic / Christian Reconstructionist)
positions/postmillennialism/strongestArg: It takes seriously the many Old Testament promises that "the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD" (Isa 11:9) within history, not only after it.
Christ already has "all authority in heaven and on earth" (Matt 28:18) and must reign "till he hath put all enemies under his feet" (1 Cor 15:25), implying victory before the end.
The kingdom parables (mustard seed, leaven) describe gradual, pervasive growth rather than collapse.
Historically it fuelled missions, revival and abolition rather than passivity, and the explosive growth of world Christianity since 1800 can be read as consistent with it.
positions/postmillennialism/strongestObj: Jesus and the apostles predict apostasy, persecution and lawlessness increasing before the end (Matt 24:9–12; Luke 18:8; 2 Tim 3:1–5).
Two world wars, the Holocaust and secularisation in its Western heartlands discredited 19th-century confidence in a Christianised civilisation.
Critics argue it easily slides into identifying the kingdom with Western progress, empire or a particular nation, and in theonomic forms into imposing Old Testament civil law.
Like amillennialism, it is accused of not doing justice to the sequence of Revelation 19–20 (Christ’s coming, then the thousand years).
positions/postmillennialism/responses/0: Postmillennialists answer that predictions of tribulation largely referred to the first century (AD 70) or describe local, not final, conditions.
positions/postmillennialism/responses/1: They distinguish biblical postmillennialism, which relies on the Spirit and gospel, from liberal progressivism, which relied on human progress; the former is not refuted by the failure of the latter.
positions/postmillennialism/responses/2: They point to the Global South, where Christianity grew from about 10 million Africans in 1900 to several hundred million today, as evidence that the leaven is still working.
positions/postmillennialism/consequences: Motivated the Concert of Prayer (1744), the modern missionary movement and voluntary societies for reform.
Shaped the 19th-century American "benevolent empire" (abolition, temperance, education) and, in secularised form, the Social Gospel.
Its collapse after 1914 opened the field to premillennialism among evangelicals and to neo-orthodoxy among mainline Protestants.
Revived since the 1970s in Christian Reconstructionism, which has influenced debates about Christian nationalism.
